exploreSites.name: Argo Tunnel & Mill
overview: The Argo complex centers on a major mining tunnel developed to drain and serve mines in the Central City–Idaho Springs region, together with the later milling and ore-handling facilities at its Idaho Springs portal.
The tunnel portal, ore bins and dump, mill, and later preservation features are related but distinct parts of the larger industrial site.

timeline.text: Development of a long drainage and haulage tunnel was undertaken to serve mines in the surrounding district.
The Argo portal became a major focal point for drainage, ore movement, and processing infrastructure at Idaho Springs.
USGS documentation recorded the dump and ore bins at the mouth of the Argo Tunnel, providing a verified operating-era view of the complex.
The industrial property transitioned from active mining infrastructure toward preservation and interpretation.
The tunnel portal and mill complex survive as prominent reminders of the engineering scale of the Clear Creek mining industry.

exploreSites.name: Silver Plume Mining & Railroad District
overview: Silver Plume developed as a major silver-mining community in Clear Creek County and later became closely associated with the railroad engineering of the Georgetown Loop corridor.
The district contains a town, depot, rail features, nearby mine components, and a broader mining landscape that together illustrate Silver Plume's development.

timeline.text: Silver discoveries and mine development drove the growth of Silver Plume as one of Colorado’s important early silver camps.
The Silver Plume Depot became the western terminus of the Colorado Central railroad line serving the community.
Rail service linked Silver Plume with Georgetown and the broader mining economy through the Georgetown Loop corridor.
Marion Post Wolcott photographed Silver Plume for the Farm Security Administration/Office of War Information.
The town and railroad landscape remain central components of the Georgetown–Silver Plume historic district.

exploreSites.location: Idaho Springs
moreHistory: Idaho Springs began as a gold-rush settlement after one of Colorado’s foundational placer discoveries. As nearby mining shifted from placer gravels to hard-rock veins, the town developed into a durable center for supplies, finance, transportation, processing, lodging, and labor.

The Miner Street commercial district contains mostly one- and two-story brick buildings with a smaller number of surviving frame structures. Their form reflects late Victorian and early twentieth-century commercial architecture rather than the rough false-front character of the earliest camp.

The district is a broad historic landscape containing many individual sites. Major features such as the Argo Tunnel & Mill, hose houses, Miner Street Bridge, and other structures remain historically connected to the larger Idaho Springs story.
The historic bird’s-eye image used here is especially useful for understanding the scale, street pattern, surrounding terrain, and relationship between the town and mining landscape.
exploreSites.name: Idaho Springs Downtown Commercial District / Historic Idaho Springs Core
overview: The historic commercial core of Idaho Springs grew from the 1859 gold rush into the principal supply and service center for the surrounding Clear Creek mining districts. Miner Street and adjoining blocks preserve the brick commercial buildings, storefronts, civic structures, and street pattern that replaced the community’s earliest tent and wood-frame settlement.

The district shows the town side of the mining landscape: hardware stores, banks, offices, saloons, markets, lodging, transportation, and services that supported mines throughout the surrounding mountains.

timeline.text: Gold discoveries at the confluence of Clear Creek and Chicago Creek triggered rapid settlement and the organization of the Jackson Mining District.
The settlement was known by several early names, including Jackson’s Diggings, Sacramento City, and Idaho/Idaho City, before the Idaho Springs name became established.
Arrival of the railroad strengthened Idaho Springs as a mining-supply and commercial center.
Many of the brick commercial buildings that define the present historic core were constructed during this period, replacing earlier frame buildings.
The downtown commercial core received formal historic-district recognition and preservation protections.

A U.S. geological survey account described the Baker mill as a significant territorial milling plant and listed Baker among active Georgetown-area lodes.
District histories continued to identify Baker as an important producer; activity later became intermittent.

exploreSites.name: Empire Mining District / Upper Union Mining District

The district is a parent landscape for Empire, North Empire, the Minnesota and Conqueror mines, Silver Mountain workings, and numerous smaller lodes. Those component sites remain separately identified in Remnant.

Lode mining expanded across the district as deeper sulfide ore bodies were developed.
District activity declined from its first boom but continued intermittently.
The district revived strongly with development of the Minnesota Mine before wartime gold-mine restrictions curtailed activity.

The generating station, water-supply penstock, and Pelton water-wheel generator sets form related but distinct parts of the historic hydroelectric system.

The present 6th Street generating plant was built.
The plant was enlarged and its penstock system was modified.
Pelton equipment was upgraded in successive phases.
The plant remains an operating generating station and is interpreted as the Georgetown Energy Museum.

Federal records document 30,623 tons shipped across recorded operating years. Modern promotional production totals are kept separate from that federal figure.
USGS ore analyses from the Phoenix document quartz with pyrite and copper-bearing sulfides, supporting the mine’s gold-silver-copper mineralization history.
Clear Creek County records independently place the modern Phoenix operation on the Snyder Lode near the Trail Creek/Stanley Road area.

The Mosch family’s official history reports acquisition in 1968 and public tours beginning in 1988; operator-reported early opening and lifetime-production figures are retained as claims rather than treated as independently verified federal totals.
exploreSites.name: Phoenix Gold Mine
overview: The Phoenix Gold Mine is a documented hard-rock mine in the Trail Creek area southwest of Idaho Springs. USGS records identify the Phoenix portal and underground workings, and federal ore analyses document gold- and silver-bearing material with copper-bearing sulfides from the mine.

The historic portal, drift-adit and lower workings are the core mining features. Later ownership and public-tour use form a separate preservation chapter, allowing the surviving mine to be interpreted without confusing modern tour infrastructure with the historic production period.

timeline.text: Federal production records include a shipment from the Phoenix Mine.
The mine again appears in documented ore-shipment records.
USGS records additional shipments during this operating period, with gold accompanied by silver, copper, lead and zinc.
The Mosch family acquired the property according to the mine’s official history.
Public mine tours began.
The historic mine is interpreted as a modern mining-history attraction while retaining its distinct underground identity.

exploreSites.location: Summit Lake / Mount Evans Scenic Byway
moreHistory: The National Register documentation identifies significance in recreation, planning and conservation, architecture, and landscape architecture.
The shelter house is one component of a larger designed setting whose historic meaning also depends on Summit Lake, the road approach, and the broader mountain landscape.
The property’s association with the Denver Mountain Parks system helps explain why a remote alpine setting received permanent visitor facilities.
exploreSites.name: Summit Lake Park / Summit Lake Shelter House
overview: Summit Lake Park is a high-elevation historic recreational landscape developed as part of the Denver Mountain Parks system and the Mount Evans Drive. The park opened in 1924.
The shelter house, lake setting, road relationship, and designed recreational landscape form a connected historic property rather than a single isolated building.

timeline.text: Summit Lake Park opened and developed in association with the Mount Evans Drive and Denver Mountain Parks system.
The park served motorists and visitors as a high-elevation recreation destination within the mountain-park network.
The park was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
The shelter and cultural landscape remain important evidence of early automobile recreation, park planning, conservation and mountain architecture.

exploreSites.name: Argentine Central Railway / Argentine & Gray's Peak Railway
overview: The Argentine Central was a three-foot narrow-gauge railway built from a connection with the Colorado & Southern at Silver Plume into the Argentine mining district near Waldorf and Mount McClellan.
The line primarily moved mining supplies and ore, while excursion traffic made its high mountain route part industrial railroad and part scenic passenger enterprise.

timeline.text: Construction began from the Colorado & Southern connection at Silver Plume.
The railway reached the Waldorf and Mount McClellan mining system.
The line carried mining materials and ore and also hosted excursion passengers.
Rail operations ended, leaving the route to survive as a historic railroad-grade landscape.
Remaining grade and route relationships document the railway’s role in connecting high-elevation mines with the Clear Creek transportation network.

exploreSites.location: Georgetown

History Colorado describes Georgetown–Silver Plume as Colorado’s most important silver camp before the 1878 Leadville strike.
Interpretation should keep Georgetown distinct from Silver Plume while showing how the two towns and their mines formed one connected historic district.
exploreSites.name: Georgetown Historic Mining Town / Silver Queen of the Rockies
overview: Georgetown developed from an 1859 gold discovery into the leading settlement of the Georgetown–Silver Plume mining district. A major silver discovery in 1864 transformed the town into a regional mining and commercial center.

The surviving town is a principal component of the Georgetown–Silver Plume National Historic Landmark district and preserves the relationship between mining, commerce, transportation, civic life, and mountain-town architecture.

timeline.text: George and David Griffith’s gold discovery launched Georgetown’s first mining boom.
A rich silver discovery triggered rapid growth and shifted the district’s economic focus.
Georgetown became the Clear Creek County seat.
The town served as the commercial and civic center of one of Colorado’s leading silver districts.
The collapse of silver prices ended the major boom period.
Georgetown survives as a major component of the Georgetown–Silver Plume National Historic Landmark district.

exploreSites.name: Henderson Mine / Henderson Molybdenum Mine
overview: The Henderson Mine is a large underground molybdenum operation at Red Mountain in Clear Creek County, developed beneath and historically distinct from the nearby Urad deposit.
Its industrial system links the underground block-cave mine on the east side of the Continental Divide with a long ore-conveyance route and a separate mill in Grand County.

timeline.text: Climax geologists discovered the Henderson ore body while drilling beneath the Urad deposit.
Molybdenum production began at the Henderson operation.
The mine used underground block-cave methods and moved ore through a long conveyor system to the mill west of the Continental Divide.
Federal and state studies documented Henderson’s geology, industrial system, and relationship to the earlier Urad mine.

A roughly 100-ton concentrating mill stood near the Lamartine tunnel portal, linking underground extraction to surface processing.
The Lamartine and Freeland mines were related principal producers in the same district but remain separate historic mine identities.
exploreSites.name: Lamartine Mine
overview: The Lamartine Mine was one of the principal lode-mining operations in the Freeland–Lamartine district, developed through a large network of shafts, tunnels, and associated ore-processing infrastructure.
Federal documentation describes more than twelve miles of workings and identifies a concentrating mill near the Lamartine tunnel portal.

timeline.text: The Lamartine property was located.
The mine produced regularly during a major operating period.
Lessees continued work after the principal early operating phase.
USGS studies documented the extensive mine network and district geology.
A federal active-mining table listed the Lamartine as a base-metal operation, confirming a later phase without implying continuous production.

Pin connections, five-panel Pratt configuration, and cantilevered sidewalks are key recognition features.

exploreSites.name: Miner Street Bridge / Bridge over Clear Creek / CC01
overview: Completed in 1902, the Miner Street Bridge carries Miner Street across Clear Creek in Idaho Springs and survives as a distinctive work of early twentieth-century bridge engineering.
The bridge is a skewed, pin-connected, five-panel steel Pratt pony truss with cantilevered sidewalks, built by Kuyes and Work.

timeline.text: Kuyes and Work completed the steel truss bridge over Clear Creek.
The bridge continued to serve the Idaho Springs street network while retaining its distinctive structural form.
The Miner Street Bridge was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.
The surviving bridge remains an identifiable transportation and engineering landmark in Idaho Springs.

exploreSites.name: Jo Reynolds Mine / Joe Reynolds Mine
overview: The Jo Reynolds Mine was a major lead-zinc-silver property in the Lawson–Dumont district, developed south of Lawson and historically distinct from the neighboring American Sisters claim group.
USGS records document extensive work from 1877 through 1907, intermittent later activity, and a large network associated with the Jo Reynolds No. 2 vein.

A shipment of eight tons of high-grade pitchblende was historically reported; USGS considered the account plausible but not fully authenticated.
Intermittent work continued after the main operating period.
USGS identified an operation around this year as the last documented working phase in its study.
Federal studies mapped and evaluated the Jo Reynolds area and its vein systems.

exploreSites.name: Seven-Thirty Mine / 7:30 Mine
overview: The Seven-Thirty Mine was an important Silver Plume mining operation associated with Heneage M. Griffin and the later Hercules & Seven-Thirty Consolidated Silver Mining Company.
Historic photographs document ore hauling and the mine’s elevated position above Silver Plume, while transportation and district records place it within the community’s larger silver-mining system.

timeline.text: The Seven-Thirty operated as one of the early Silver Plume mining interests.
Seven-Thirty, Hercules, and East Roe interests were consolidated into the Hercules & Seven-Thirty Consolidated Silver Mining Company.
Ore was hauled from the mine for transport and processing, as documented in a site-specific historic stereograph.
A panorama made from the Seven-Thirty Mine documented the mine’s relationship to Silver Plume and the surrounding landscape.
The mine remains an important identification point within the historic Silver Plume mining landscape.

The mine should be interpreted as one component of Silver Plume’s larger mining landscape while preserving its separate operating identity.
exploreSites.name: Smuggler Mine / Silver Plume Smuggler Mine
overview: The Silver Plume Smuggler Mine was a long-lived polymetallic operation west of town, producing gold, silver, lead, and zinc from the 1890s into the 1950s.
A largely intact timber-and-steel headframe gives the property an unusually strong surface identification anchor within the broader Silver Plume mining landscape.

timeline.text: Documented operation of the Silver Plume Smuggler began during this decade.
Colorado mining records identified the Hollingsworth Mining Company property west of Silver Plume as the Smuggler Mine.
Mining continued across multiple phases, producing gold, silver, lead, and zinc.
Operations ended while substantial surface infrastructure, including the headframe, survived.
The preserved mining landscape remains distinguished by its timber-and-steel headframe and community preservation history.

moreHistory: The Urad was an earlier molybdenum operation in the same mountain setting later associated with the Henderson Mine, but the two should remain separate site identities.
Federal reporting documents the wartime lease, Defense Plant Corporation development, mill construction, and the mine’s extensive underground development.
Clear Creek County later described the closed Urad facilities as reclaimed; this historical status does not imply public access.
exploreSites.name: Urad Mine / URAD Molybdenum Mine
overview: The Urad Mine was a major molybdenum property in Woods Creek Valley, developed first by the Primos Chemical Company and later expanded during World War II.
Its documented landscape combined extensive underground workings with a 200-ton-per-day mill, and later reclamation distinguishes the historic operation from the adjacent Henderson Mine.

timeline.text: Primos Chemical Company began development of the Urad molybdenum property.
The first documented operating phase developed the deposit.
Molybdenum Corporation of America leased the mine and began wartime development under the Defense Plant Corporation.
Mining and milling operated with a 200-ton-per-day concentration mill.
USGS reported roughly 20,000 feet of underground development together with extensive drilling.
The historic Urad facilities were closed and reclaimed while the neighboring Henderson operation remained a distinct mine.

moreHistory: Edward J. Wilcox’s Waldorf Company linked mine development, milling, railroad service, and the Santiago aerial tramway in one industrial landscape.
The settlement’s growth reflected both mining and visitor traffic, making Waldorf more than an isolated mine site.
Waldorf and the nearby Santiago Mine and Mill are related district resources but should remain separate site identities.
exploreSites.name: Waldorf Mining Camp / Waldorf Mine & Mill Complex
overview: Waldorf was an Argentine district mining camp organized around Edward J. Wilcox’s tunnel and concentration mill, with railroad service and an aerial tramway tying the site to nearby ore sources.
A mill erected in 1905 and a post office granted in 1906 mark the rapid development of a small industrial community supported by mining, transportation, and tourist traffic.

timeline.text: The Waldorf Company erected a concentration mill at the tunnel.
Ore from the Santiago Mine reached the Waldorf mill by aerial tramway.
A post office was granted under the name Waldorf as the camp expanded.
Railroad service, milling, mining, and tourist traffic sustained the camp.
Industrial activity declined, leaving a connected mine, mill, camp, tramway, and railroad landscape.

exploreSites.name: Grizzly Mine / Grizzly Gulch Mine
exploreSites.location: Grizzly Gulch, historic Argentine Mining District
overview: Grizzly Mine was a long-lived high-country operation in the historic Argentine Mining District, working intermittently from the early 1870s into the late 1950s for silver, lead, zinc, and earlier gold-bearing prospects.

The site’s later history is also significant: scientific investigation of mine waste led to a reclamation project completed in 2023, changing portions of the visible mining landscape while addressing water, waste, stream, road, and unstable-structure concerns.

timeline.text: Mining activity began in Grizzly Gulch during the district’s early gold and silver development.
The National vein became important for silver- and lead-bearing ore, and the mine operated intermittently into the twentieth century.
A fire affected the operation near the end of its productive era.
Documented mining activity ended.
A reevaluation concluded that remaining ore was not economic to develop.
The site was sampled and assessed as part of a mine-waste and watershed investigation.
Reclamation was completed, consolidating waste and addressing drainage, stream, road, and unstable surface features while considering cultural resources.

features.name: Historic Grizzly Mine Workings
features.note: Historic sources document intermittent mining from the early 1870s into the late 1950s.

features.name: National Vein Workings
features.note: Later mine history identifies the National vein as an important silver- and lead-bearing target.

features.name: Mine-Waste and Reclamation Area
features.note: USGS and project sources document mine-waste study and reclamation completed in 2023.

moreHistory: Grizzly Mine’s story spans both nineteenth-century mineral development and twenty-first-century watershed restoration. Historic accounts describe intermittent work and changing commodity emphasis rather than a single continuous operating period.
The 1956 fire and the uneconomic 1977–78 reevaluation help explain why renewed large-scale mining did not follow the earlier operating era.

Modern reclamation consolidated mine waste, diverted water, repaired stream and floodplain areas, rehabilitated roads, and treated unstable surface structures. Those changes mean the present landscape does not necessarily preserve every feature described in older mining records.

features.note: The portal is the principal surface opening of the long drainage and haulage tunnel.

features.name: Ore Bins and Dump Area

features.name: Argo Mill

identificationSites.location: Idaho Springs
moreHistory: The Argo was not simply a mine entrance. Its historical role depended on its relationship to a much larger network of underground workings, drainage, ore handling, transportation, and processing.
The portal, dump and ore-bin system, mill buildings, and later interpretive features represent different phases and functions within the Argo complex.
A verified USGS image from Professional Paper 94 shows the dump and ore bins at the tunnel mouth and provides a strong historical reference for interpreting the site.
identificationSites.name: Argo Tunnel & Mill
overview: The Argo complex centers on a major mining tunnel developed to drain and serve mines in the Central City–Idaho Springs region, together with the later milling and ore-handling facilities at its Idaho Springs portal.
The tunnel portal, ore bins and dump, mill, and later preservation features are related but distinct parts of the larger industrial site.

timeline.text: Development of a long drainage and haulage tunnel was undertaken to serve mines in the surrounding district.
The Argo portal became a major focal point for drainage, ore movement, and processing infrastructure at Idaho Springs.
USGS documentation recorded the dump and ore bins at the mouth of the Argo Tunnel, providing a verified operating-era view of the complex.
The industrial property transitioned from active mining infrastructure toward preservation and interpretation.
The tunnel portal and mill complex survive as prominent reminders of the engineering scale of the Clear Creek mining industry.

identificationSites.name: Silver Plume Mining & Railroad District
overview: Silver Plume developed as a major silver-mining community in Clear Creek County and later became closely associated with the railroad engineering of the Georgetown Loop corridor.
The district contains a town, depot, rail features, nearby mine components, and a broader mining landscape that together illustrate Silver Plume's development.

timeline.text: Silver discoveries and mine development drove the growth of Silver Plume as one of Colorado’s important early silver camps.
The Silver Plume Depot became the western terminus of the Colorado Central railroad line serving the community.
Rail service linked Silver Plume with Georgetown and the broader mining economy through the Georgetown Loop corridor.
Marion Post Wolcott photographed Silver Plume for the Farm Security Administration/Office of War Information.
The town and railroad landscape remain central components of the Georgetown–Silver Plume historic district.

features.name: Miner Street Commercial Core
features.note: The principal surviving commercial spine of the historic mining town, dominated by brick buildings dating from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

features.name: Railroad-Era Town Development
features.note: Rail access beginning in 1877 strengthened Idaho Springs as a regional mining supply and service center.

identificationSites.location: Idaho Springs
moreHistory: Idaho Springs began as a gold-rush settlement after one of Colorado’s foundational placer discoveries. As nearby mining shifted from placer gravels to hard-rock veins, the town developed into a durable center for supplies, finance, transportation, processing, lodging, and labor.

The Miner Street commercial district contains mostly one- and two-story brick buildings with a smaller number of surviving frame structures. Their form reflects late Victorian and early twentieth-century commercial architecture rather than the rough false-front character of the earliest camp.

The district is a broad historic landscape containing many individual sites. Major features such as the Argo Tunnel & Mill, hose houses, Miner Street Bridge, and other structures remain historically connected to the larger Idaho Springs story.
The historic bird’s-eye image used here is especially useful for understanding the scale, street pattern, surrounding terrain, and relationship between the town and mining landscape.
identificationSites.name: Idaho Springs Downtown Commercial District / Historic Idaho Springs Core
overview: The historic commercial core of Idaho Springs grew from the 1859 gold rush into the principal supply and service center for the surrounding Clear Creek mining districts. Miner Street and adjoining blocks preserve the brick commercial buildings, storefronts, civic structures, and street pattern that replaced the community’s earliest tent and wood-frame settlement.

The district shows the town side of the mining landscape: hardware stores, banks, offices, saloons, markets, lodging, transportation, and services that supported mines throughout the surrounding mountains.

timeline.text: Gold discoveries at the confluence of Clear Creek and Chicago Creek triggered rapid settlement and the organization of the Jackson Mining District.
The settlement was known by several early names, including Jackson’s Diggings, Sacramento City, and Idaho/Idaho City, before the Idaho Springs name became established.
Arrival of the railroad strengthened Idaho Springs as a mining-supply and commercial center.
Many of the brick commercial buildings that define the present historic core were constructed during this period, replacing earlier frame buildings.
The downtown commercial core received formal historic-district recognition and preservation protections.

identificationSites.name: Bakerville Mining Camp / Bakerville

District histories continued to identify Baker as an important producer; activity later became intermittent.

timeline.text: Gold-bearing oxidized material was discovered and early miners worked decomposed surface material and placers.
Lode mining expanded across the district as deeper sulfide ore bodies were developed.
District activity declined from its first boom but continued intermittently.
The district revived strongly with development of the Minnesota Mine before wartime gold-mine restrictions curtailed activity.

A C&S renumbering assigned the car the No. 70 identity preserved today.
Coach No. 70 was moved to Idaho Springs with Engine No. 60 as the Clear Creek narrow-gauge line was being abandoned.
